prose:
# Trump says he would meet Putin and Xi without Zelensky

One pattern links today's news. Leaders bargain and wait for dates that suit them. Meanwhile, the people with the least say carry the costs. Ukraine loses interceptors and warnings while Trump courts Putin. Saudi Arabia's private firms take a war bill that high oil prices do not cover. Two elections set the clock for a new strike on Iran. France answers its protesters with police and with money for damaged shops, but not with lower prices. In Asia, pension funds and state banks buy the chip stocks that foreign funds sell.

## Russia pounds Kyiv as Trump courts Putin

A month ago, the US held a strong lever over Russia. Trump signed the Graham Act on Sept. 18, and its sanctions and tariffs on Russia were due to start on Oct. 18. Then came an Oct. 9 phone call between Trump and Putin. The call produced a deal and an offer. Under the deal, Russia sells diesel to the US and other markets: about 300,000 tonnes this month, rising toward about 1 million tonnes a month. The offer came from Putin: a three-way meeting with Trump and China's leader, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific summit in Shenzhen on Nov. 18-19. On Oct. 16, Trump waived nearly all of the Graham Act's sanctions and tariffs, with no end date.

On Oct. 19, Trump said that he would meet Putin and Xi, with or without Zelensky. He said that it was time for someone else to negotiate for Ukraine. Later he said that the meeting would be about nuclear weapons, not Ukraine, and that Russia's conduct toward Ukraine was fairly normal.

The same day showed the other side of the change. The Washington Post reported that allied requests to send their US-made Patriot interceptors to Ukraine still wait for a decision from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Allies need US approval for these transfers, even when Europe pays. A Ukrainian official told the paper that Ukraine has only a couple of Patriot interceptors left. Zelensky also says that no timely US launch warning came before Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv on Oct. 12 and on Oct. 19.

Overnight into Oct. 19, Russia fired about 270 drones and missiles at Ukraine. Sixteen were ballistic missiles, aimed mainly at Kyiv. Ukraine shot down 243 drones and four cruise missiles, but none of the ballistic missiles. The strikes hit 28 substations and other energy sites in 11 regions, and at least 550,000 families lost power. A 21-year-old woman died in Kyiv. Russia says that it hit military and industrial sites. Later that day, a Russian drone hit the central park of Nova Vodolaha, a small town in the Kharkiv region. It killed six people, among them a one-year-old girl in her stroller and her mother.

The mechanism is a shift of leverage. Putin pairs the deal with the offer. The deal gives Trump Russian diesel, which can cool US fuel prices before the midterm elections on Nov. 3. The offer moves the talks to a summit of great powers, where Ukraine has no seat. The waiver removes the main penalty that Congress gave Trump, so the pressure now runs toward Ukraine, not Russia. Ukraine also depends on two US services that it cannot quickly replace. The first is approval for Patriot transfers, which the US can slow just by not signing. The second is US launch warnings, which give civilians minutes to reach a shelter. Ukraine reads both delays as pressure to settle and to stop its strikes on Russian refineries. Whatever the cause, Ukraine now knows that a service it cannot replace can stop without notice.

The strongest competing reading is that nothing is settled. The Kremlin says that there is no agenda, and China says that it has no information. In October 2025, Trump announced a summit with Putin in Budapest after a phone call, and the plan collapsed within about a week. The Pentagon refused nothing and still approves other aid to Ukraine. Paperwork, or the demand for interceptors in the Iran war, can explain the delay. The claim of a couple of interceptors left comes from one unnamed official. Secretary of State Marco Rubio says that intelligence sharing never paused, and he blames a technical fault that US European Command investigates. Even on that reading, Ukraine goes into winter short of its main defense against ballistic missiles.

UBIK's read is that both sides want a meeting, but its form is fragile. Both leaders plan to be in Shenzhen, and both say that they are willing to meet. Trump's envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, meet Zelensky in Oslo on Oct. 20. Witkoff then plans talks with Putin in Moscow, which gives a channel to arrange a meeting. But China, the host, does not commit, and it calls three-way nuclear talks unfair because its arsenal is much smaller. It reportedly fears that a great-power meeting on Ukraine or nuclear arms can overshadow the Shenzhen summit and upset Europe. Trump may also prefer the December G20 summit in the US. At Da Nang in 2017 and Buenos Aires in 2018, planned Trump–Putin meetings at big summits shrank to short, informal talks. [UBIK puts at 0.52 the chance that Trump and Putin hold a formal, in-person meeting by the Shenzhen summit next month](/forecasts/q_20261020_02), because both men want it, but China's caution and past summits show that it can shrink to a handshake.

## Saudi Arabia puts off its investor conference under Houthi fire

Yemen's 2022 truce collapsed in July. On July 20, the Houthis declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia, in answer to the blockade on the part of Yemen that they hold. Saudi Arabia now bombs Houthi territory and backs a government push toward Sanaa. The Houthis, allies of Iran, answer with missiles and drones at Saudi cities, airports and oil sites. Houthi strikes on Riyadh's airport on Oct. 8, 10 and 11 killed at least 16 people. The airport closed for a week and opened again on Oct. 18.

[Will Saudi Arabia's private businesses shrink this month? UBIK puts it at 15 percent.](/forecasts/q_20261020_01)

## Hegseth flies to Israel as talk of bombing Iran grows

The US and Israel opened their war on Iran on Feb. 28 with strikes that killed Iran's supreme leader. Iran answered with missiles and drones and shut Hormuz. After that, pauses alternated with US air campaigns. The last US strikes came on Sept. 1, on about 100 Revolutionary Guard coastal sites, and a US naval blockade of Iran continues. On Oct. 8, Trump promised no attack on Iran before the midterms. Since that promise, Iran attacked ships faster than at any time in the war. JINSA, a US think tank, counts 26 attacks in October through Oct. 19, with two ships sunk. Iran says that Hormuz stays shut until the US accepts its plan to reopen it, and the talks are deadlocked.

[Will America or Israel bomb Iran again before Thanksgiving? UBIK puts it at 55 percent.](/forecasts/q_20261020_03)

## France imposes curfews after riots, and the unrest reaches Italy

France's unrest began on Sept. 21, when high-school students blocked their schools over missing teachers, crowded classes and run-down buildings. By early October, two more grievances joined the school protests. Diesel cost about 2.35 euros a litre, because the Iran war keeps oil expensive. And Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu proposed 54 billion euros of savings in next year's budget. On Oct. 17, an open call online brought students, former Yellow Vests, union members and many others onto the streets. The Interior Ministry counted 550,000 people, and the CGT union counted 800,000. The authorities had expected at most 200,000.

[Will Saturday's protests in France draw less than half last week's crowd? UBIK puts it at 80 percent.](/forecasts/q_20261020_04)

[Will France's November strike draw fewer marchers than Saturday's protests? UBIK puts it at 68 percent.](/forecasts/q_20261018_05)

## Foreign funds sell Asian chip stocks as AI doubts grow

Through 2026, AI chip shares rose on the belief that AI spending would keep growing. Then the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, the main gauge of US chip stocks, fell for eight sessions in a row through Oct. 16 and lost 15.7%. It was the longest losing run since October 2008. On Oct. 19, the US chip index rose 1.61%, led by memory-chip makers. But the rally was thin: nearly two-thirds of the stocks in the S&P 500 fell.

[Will Taiwan's dollar keep falling despite its central bank's warning? It settled yes.](/forecasts/q_20261019_05)

forecasts.claim: Will Trump and Putin meet in person by next month's China summit?
forecasts.resolution_source: White House and Kremlin (kremlin.ru, Peskov or Ushakov) statements; Reuters and AP reporting
forecasts.resolution_rule: Yes if, between Oct. 20 and Nov. 20, 2026, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin hold an in-person meeting or talks anywhere, including at the APEC leaders' summit in Shenzhen on Nov. 18-19. The meeting may be one-on-one or together with Xi Jinping or others in a three-way format. It counts if the White House or the Kremlin describes it as a meeting or talks between the two leaders, or if both Reuters and AP report that the two held a meeting or talks. It must be held apart from sessions, meals or photos open to all APEC leaders: a conversation during those does not count, whatever either side calls it. A handshake, greeting or brief exchange counts only if the White House or the Kremlin calls it a meeting or talks. Phone and video calls do not count. Reports published by Nov. 23 about a meeting held by Nov. 20 count. No if no qualifying meeting held by Nov. 20 is reported by Nov. 23, including if either leader skips the summit or leaves without one. Void if the APEC leaders' summit in Shenzhen is called off or postponed past Nov. 20 and no qualifying meeting has been held by then.

history.why: Both leaders will attend and say they are willing, but nothing is agreed.

forecasts.reasoning: Trump and Putin both plan to attend the Shenzhen summit on Nov. 18-19, and both say that they are willing to meet. Trump waived the Graham Act's sanctions and tariffs and accepted a Russian diesel deal, which shows that he wants to engage Russia. Witkoff and Kushner meet Zelensky in Oslo, and Witkoff plans talks with Putin in Moscow, so a channel exists to arrange a meeting. But nothing is agreed. The Kremlin says that there is no agenda, US officials say that Trump did not formally agree, and China, the host, does not commit. China reportedly fears that the meeting will overshadow its summit and upset Europe. Trump may prefer the December G20 summit in the US. At Da Nang in 2017 and Buenos Aires in 2018, planned Trump–Putin meetings at summits shrank to short informal talks. Only a formal meeting that the White House or the Kremlin calls talks counts, not a greeting at a meal, a session or a group photo.
forecasts.uncertainty: The main uncertainty is whether contact in Shenzhen becomes a formal meeting or only a short informal talk. China's position and Trump's reaction to new Russian strikes on civilians are also unclear.
forecasts.rises_if: The White House or the Kremlin announces a formal two-way or three-way meeting in Shenzhen, or China agrees to host it.
forecasts.falls_if: Trump moves the meeting to the December G20, China refuses to host it, or a large Russian strike on civilians turns US politics against a meeting.

forecasts.claim: Will Saudi Arabia's private businesses shrink this month?
forecasts.resolution_source: S&P Global, Riyad Bank Saudi Arabia PMI press release for October 2026 (pmi.spglobal.com), expected around Nov. 3-4, 2026
forecasts.resolution_rule: Yes if the headline seasonally adjusted Riyad Bank Saudi Arabia PMI for October 2026, as first published by S&P Global, is below 50.0. No if it is 50.0 or higher. Later revisions are ignored. If S&P Global has not published the October 2026 reading by the end of Nov. 5, 2026, the question is void.

forecasts.claim: Will America or Israel bomb Iran again before Thanksgiving?
forecasts.resolution_source: Official statements by the US Department of Defense, US Central Command or the White House, or by the Israel Defense Forces or the Israeli Prime Minister's Office; or reporting by at least two of Reuters, the Associated Press and Axios.
forecasts.resolution_rule: Yes if, between 2026-10-20T09:00Z and 2026-11-25T23:59Z, US or Israeli forces carry out at least one air, missile or drone strike on a target on Iranian territory: the mainland, Iranian-held islands, or ships moored at an Iranian port or base. A strike launched at such a target counts whether or not Iranian defences intercept it. The strike must be acknowledged by one of the named governments or reported as a US or Israeli strike by at least two of the named outlets, in their own reporting or citing US or Israeli officials; Iranian accusations alone do not count, nor do reports the outlets have retracted by the end of 2026-11-28. Not counted: blockade enforcement or other action against vessels at sea, including inside Iran's territorial waters; interception of Iranian missiles, drones or boats; strikes on Iranian-backed groups or Iranian assets outside Iran; cyberattacks; and sabotage or killings inside Iran that neither government acknowledges and the named outlets do not report as a US or Israeli strike. A strike before Nov. 3 counts the same as one after it. Acknowledgements and reports published up to the end of 2026-11-28 count for strikes within the window. If no qualifying strike in the window has been acknowledged or reported by the end of 2026-11-28, the question resolves No.

forecasts.claim: Will Saturday's protests in France draw less than half last week's crowd?
forecasts.resolution_source: French Interior Ministry national count of demonstrators for Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, as published by the ministry or relayed from it by AFP, Le Monde or franceinfo
forecasts.resolution_rule: Yes if the Interior Ministry's nationwide count of protesters in France for Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, is below 275,000, which is half its count of 550,000 for Oct. 17. No if it is 275,000 or more. Use the latest full-day national figure the ministry publishes by 23:59 Paris time on Oct. 31, 2026; if it publishes only an intraday figure, use the latest one published by then. Ignore later revisions and any count by unions, organizers or independent counters. If the ministry publishes a national figure for Oct. 24, that figure settles the question whatever else happens. If it publishes none by the deadline: void if the national protest day was moved from Oct. 24 to a later date; otherwise Yes, including when the calls are withdrawn or banned or the protests are too scattered for a national count.

forecasts.claim: Will Taiwan's dollar keep falling despite its central bank's warning?
forecasts.resolution_source: Central Bank of the Republic of China (Taiwan), New Taiwan Dollar Exchange Rates (Interbank Spot Market Closing Rates, NTD/USD), daily series on cbc.gov.tw (Foreign Exchange Historical Data, Daily); if the bank's series is unavailable, the same Taipei Forex Inc. 4 p.m. official close as reported by Taiwan's Central News Agency (cna.com.tw).
forecasts.resolution_rule: Yes if the central bank's published official closing rate for any Taipei trading day from Oct. 20 through Nov. 2, 2026 inclusive is weaker than NT$32.500 per US dollar, meaning a number above 32.500. No if every official close for those days is 32.500 or stronger (32.500 itself counts as No). Each day's close as first published counts; later revisions do not change the result. Intraday highs and lows, offshore non-deliverable forward rates and bank counter rates do not count. Days the Taipei market is closed, including typhoon closures, are skipped, and a day with no published close is treated as closed. Closes must be published by Nov. 9, 2026 to count. Void only if the Taipei market publishes no official close for any day in the window. Reference: the Oct. 19 close was 32.445 after an intraday low of 32.55.

history.why: The central bank defends 32.50 at the close, against record foreign outflows.

evidence.quote: The U.S. dollar rose against the Taiwan dollar Tuesday, gaining NT$0.172 to close at NT$32.617.

forecasts.reasoning: Only the central bank's official 4 p.m. close counts. On Oct. 19 the Taiwan dollar went past 32.50 per US dollar during trading but closed at 32.445, about 0.17% short of the line. Foreign investors sold a net 19.4 billion US dollars of Taiwanese shares in the week of Oct. 12-16, and the central bank links the fall to those outflows. But the central bank pulled the close back from 32.50 late in the session in July, in August, and on Oct. 16 and 19. On Oct. 19 it also said in mid-session that it will step in when necessary, and it has about 600 billion US dollars of reserves.
forecasts.uncertainty: The distance to the line is very small and the selling is at record levels, so a free market would probably cross it. The open question is whether the central bank keeps a hard line or lets the Taiwan dollar fall slowly to save reserves. US tech results and the Fed meeting on Oct. 27-28 fall inside the window.
forecasts.rises_if: The Fed signals an October rate increase, US tech shares fall further, or foreign selling of Taiwanese shares continues at record pace.
forecasts.falls_if: Foreign funds return to Taiwanese shares, US chip stocks recover, or exporters sell US dollars into the market.

forecasts.resolution_source: French Interior Ministry nationwide count of demonstrators for the Nov. 5, 2026 inter-union day of strikes and marches (CFDT, CGT, FO, Unsa, FSU), as published by the ministry or reported from it by AFP, Le Monde, franceinfo or Le Figaro.
forecasts.resolution_rule: YES if the Interior Ministry's nationwide demonstrator count for the Nov. 5, 2026 inter-union day, published by the end of Nov. 12, 2026 (Paris time), is below 550,000, the ministry's count for Oct. 17, 2026. NO if it is 550,000 or more, or if the ministry publishes no nationwide figure for the day by then. Union, organizer or independent counts and Paris-only or other partial figures do not count. The threshold stays 550,000 even if the ministry later revises its Oct. 17 figure. If the day is moved to another date no later than Nov. 6, 2026, use the ministry's count for that date. VOID only if the day is cancelled or moved to a date after Nov. 6, 2026.

currents.title: Trump eases Russia sanctions and leans on Kyiv as Putin pitches a summit with Xi
currents.mechanism: Washington is easing pressure on Moscow and tightening it on Kyiv at the same time. Trump has switched off the Graham Act penalties and is buying Russian diesel to cool fuel prices and keep Putin talking. Meanwhile the Pentagon has not signed off on allied Patriot transfers, and Ukraine says U.S. warnings of ballistic launches have faltered. Washington denies withholding anything, but Kyiv reads both as pressure to settle and to stop hitting Russian refineries. Russia is hitting Ukraine's grid harder as interceptors run short, and is steering the diplomacy toward a leaders' meeting in Shenzhen on Nov. 18-19 where Ukraine would not be at the table. Next steps: Witkoff and Kushner's Oslo talks with Zelensky on Oct. 20, the Shenzhen summit on Nov. 18-19, the waiver review Rubio put at up to 60 days, and the December G20 in the U.S.

developments.title: Trump says he would meet Putin and Xi in Shenzhen without Zelensky, then recasts it as nuclear talks
developments.what_happened: Prior situation: in an Oct. 9 phone call, Putin proposed that he, Trump and Xi Jinping meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders' summit in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 18-19. All three were already expected there: Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said on Sept. 30 that Putin would attend as planned, and Trump and Xi confirmed their intention to attend after their September summit at the White House. The same call produced a deal for Russia to sell diesel to the U.S. and other markets, about 300,000 tonnes (roughly 2.3 million barrels) this month and rising toward about 1 million tonnes (7.6 million barrels) a month, under a Treasury license running through April. On Oct. 16 Trump signed an order waiving nearly all the sanctions and tariffs of the Graham Act, the Russia sanctions law he signed on Sept. 18, two days before they were due to take effect on Oct. 18. The waiver has no end date; Rubio has described it as a review of up to 60 days. New in this window: the Wall Street Journal reported the summit proposal on Oct. 19, with a senior U.S. official saying Trump had not yet agreed. Later that day, leaving the White House for a campaign event in Kansas, Trump told reporters he would meet Putin and Xi and do anything he could to end the war whether or not Zelensky was there. He said Zelensky should have settled the war long ago and it was time for someone else to negotiate for Ukraine. In further remarks he said the meeting would be about nuclear weapons and denuclearization rather than Ukraine, and that Russia was behaving fairly normally toward Ukraine. He also defended the diesel deal as a way to avoid driving Russia from the negotiating table. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the idea came up because all three leaders may be at the summit, but nobody has put forward concrete proposals on the meeting or its agenda, and a final settlement is impossible without someone from Kyiv. Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said she had no in
developments.why_it_matters: For the first time, a U.S. president is openly willing to discuss ending the war at a table with Russia and China while Ukraine is absent. The offer arrives as Washington has dropped the sanctions Congress built to pressure Moscow and is buying Russian fuel. Trump's shifting account of the subject leaves open whether Ukraine's future or arms control would be negotiated in Shenzhen. European capitals and Taiwan have voiced alarm that the three powers could decide matters over their heads.
developments.plain_summary: In an Oct. 9 phone call, Putin suggested that he, Trump and China's Xi meet next month in Shenzhen, China. All three are already due there for a big Asia-Pacific summit on Nov. 18 and 19, but Ukraine would not be in the room. On Monday Trump said he'd do it, with or without Zelensky, and said it was time for someone else to negotiate for Ukraine. Later he said the meeting would really be about nuclear weapons. The Kremlin says nothing is settled, and China says it knows nothing. The same Oct. 9 call produced a deal for Russia to sell diesel to America. A week later, Trump switched off almost all of a new law meant to punish Russia. Kyiv says a meeting about Ukraine without Ukraine only encourages Putin, and Zelensky is meeting Trump's envoys in Oslo instead.

developments.title: Pentagon sits on allied Patriot transfers as a Ukrainian official says only a couple of interceptors are left
developments.what_happened: Prior situation: under Trump, the U.S. sells Patriot interceptors to Ukraine rather than giving them, and European allies pay for American weapons for Kyiv through NATO's PURL purchase arrangement. Allies that own U.S.-made Patriots need Washington's approval to pass them on to a third country. Zelensky has said deliveries are down to about 12 interceptors a month, roughly a quarter of the Biden-era rate. Last week he offered to stop Ukraine's strikes on Russian diesel plants in exchange for more Patriots, and Washington did not commit to sending them. New in this window: the Washington Post reported on Oct. 19 that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had neither approved nor rejected requests to transfer Patriot interceptors held by allies. A Ukrainian official told the paper Ukraine had only a couple left. The Pentagon said Hegseth continues to approve other U.S. assistance to Ukraine. On Oct. 19 Zelensky told a visiting U.S. congressional delegation that interceptors European allies had already paid for were being held back. He said a political decision had been made to slow the support Ukraine receives. After the overnight strike, he ordered his defense and foreign ministries and his office to press partners to speed up air-defense supplies, citing unfulfilled agreements and delays at the U.S. Defense Department.
developments.why_it_matters: Patriots are Ukraine's main defense against Russia's ballistic missiles. In the Oct. 19 attack, Ukraine intercepted none of the ballistic missiles fired at Kyiv. Russia's campaign against the power grid is intensifying just as winter approaches.
developments.plain_summary: Ukraine's best weapon against Russia's fastest missiles is the American-made Patriot. Under Trump, the U.S. sells Patriot missiles rather than giving them, and European allies often pay. Allies that own Patriots need Washington's permission to pass them to Ukraine, and the Washington Post reports that Defense Secretary Hegseth simply hasn't signed, neither yes nor no. A Ukrainian official says the country is down to a couple of the missiles. Zelensky told visiting American lawmakers that missiles Europe already paid for are being held back on purpose. The Pentagon says it is still approving other aid.

developments.title: Zelensky says no warning came before the ballistic strike on Kyiv; Rubio says intelligence sharing never paused
developments.what_happened: Prior situation: when Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv late on Oct. 12, killing two women, sirens sounded only after the strike began. Axios, the Financial Times and CNN reported that Witkoff and Kushner had threatened to suspend intelligence sharing. U.S. sources variously blamed bad weather or said the launch was not seen, and other sources denied any decision to cut sharing. On Oct. 18 Zelensky told NBC that warnings had been cut off for three days and then restored. New in this window: Zelensky said that before Russia's Oct. 19 ballistic attack on Kyiv, Ukraine again received no timely warning from its partners. A senior Ukrainian official dismissed weather explanations and said such a breakdown had never happened before. Visiting Uzbekistan, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there had been no pause in intelligence sharing. He attributed any gap to a technical problem under investigation by U.S. European Command and urged Zelensky to focus on ending the war. Zelensky also complained of restricted access to the Starshield satellite network and said Starlink and Starshield terminals stop working at speeds of about 130-161 km/h at the front.
developments.why_it_matters: Ballistic missiles reach Kyiv within minutes, and U.S. launch warnings are what give civilians time to shelter and air defenses time to react. If the warnings are faltering while Patriots are scarce, Ukraine's cities are exposed on both fronts at once.
developments.plain_summary: Ukraine also relies on America to warn it when Russia launches ballistic missiles, which leave people only minutes to get to shelter. Zelensky says no warning came before Monday's strike on Kyiv, just as none came before one on Oct. 12, and his officials say that has never happened before. Secretary of State Rubio says intelligence sharing never paused, and blames a technical glitch the U.S. military is investigating. If the gap is real, it is opening just as Washington presses Kyiv to settle.

developments.title: Russia's overnight barrage hits Kyiv and the power grid, and a drone kills six in a Kharkiv-region park
developments.what_happened: Prior situation: Russia has kept up a campaign against Ukraine's power system. Ukrainian officials count 2,147 attacks on energy facilities since July 16, and Zelensky counts 76 strikes on the energy sector since Trump announced an energy truce on Oct. 11. On Oct. 16, according to Ukraine's energy ministry, Russia shifted to hitting transmission towers and power lines, causing voltage drops in Kyiv that disrupted water supply and electric transport. Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian oil sites and sent more than 1,000 drones toward oil facilities near St. Petersburg on the night of Oct. 17-18. New in this window: overnight into Oct. 19, Russia launched about 270 drones and missiles, including 16 ballistic missiles aimed mainly at Kyiv and its region. Ukraine's air force said it downed 243 drones and four cruise missiles but none of the ballistic missiles. Twenty-eight substations and other energy sites were hit across 11 regions, and at least 550,000 families lost power. In Kyiv, a 21-year-old woman was killed and eight people were injured. A metro station, a clinic in a 25-story residential building and a school were damaged, and telecom operator Datagroup said one of its data centers was destroyed. In Irpin, outside Kyiv, people including children were injured and three were reported missing. Later on Oct. 19, a Russian attack drone struck the central park of Nova Vodolaha, a town of about 10,000 in the Kharkiv region. It killed six people, including a 1-year-old girl in her stroller, her mother and an 11-year-old girl; some officials put the number of children killed at three. Fifteen people were injured, seven of them children. Zelensky called it an atrocity and urged the U.S. to enforce the Graham Act. Russia's Defense Ministry said it struck military-industrial sites, missile and drone storage and data centers.
developments.why_it_matters: It was one of Russia's broadest air assaults in months. It landed the same day Trump said Russia was behaving fairly normally toward Ukraine and offered to meet Putin, and it shows what a shortage of interceptors and warnings means on the ground.
developments.plain_summary: Overnight into Monday, Russia fired about 270 drones and missiles at Ukraine, including 16 ballistic missiles aimed mostly at Kyiv. Ukraine shot down most of the drones but not one of the ballistic missiles. Twenty-eight substations and other power sites were hit across 11 regions, and more than half a million families lost electricity. A 21-year-old woman was killed in Kyiv. Later that day in Nova Vodolaha, a small town near Kharkiv, a Russian drone hit a park and killed six people, among them a one-year-old girl in her stroller and her mother. Russia says it hit military targets. With winter weeks away, Ukraine says it is running out of the missiles that can stop these attacks.
